articles.title_orig: Egypt’s US Military Aid: How China Views Its Future and Cairo’s Strategic Choices
articles.title_zh: Egypt’s US Military Aid: How China Views Its Future and Cairo’s Strategic Choices
articles.content_orig:
China approaches the issue of US military aid to Egypt—amounting to approximately $1.3 billion annually—with a calm, pragmatic perspective. It views this aid as a diminishingly effective tool of American influence, opening a strategic window for Beijing to strengthen its defense and economic partnership with Cairo without seeking direct confrontation to completely replace Washington. Recently, Egyptian-American relations have faced escalating tensions and pressures due to the growing rapprochement between Cairo and Beijing. The period between August and September 2026 witnessed potential US threats and warnings regarding a review or even a cut in the annual military aid Egypt receives (estimated at around $1.3 billion) against the backdrop of this accelerating strategic, economic, and military cooperation with China, according to reports in Hebrew media outlets such as Israel Hayom. We can link the growing military ties between Cairo and Beijing to the strained military relations between Cairo and Washington, as follows:
–             First: The impact of the Egyptian-Chinese military rapprochement on the details of the tension and the American threats to reduce military aid to Egypt
1) Egyptian-Chinese rapprochement: Partnerships and reciprocal visits between the Egyptian and Chinese leaderships have intensified (including visits and agreements with Chinese President Xi Jinping), which has raised concerns and resentment within the American administration and circles in Washington.
2) The pressure tactic (military aid): Some within the American administration have threatened to reconsider military aid or even cut it off as a pressure tactic to prevent Egypt from deviating from the American sphere of influence or expanding its technical and military cooperation with China and other international powers.

3) The Egyptian Position: Cairo affirms through official statements and positions that it is not seeking to replace one ally with another but rather is pursuing a policy of diversifying its sources of arms and economic and military support to enhance its independence and achieve balance in its foreign relations.
4) Divergent Positions in Washington: Conversely, some pragmatic statements have emerged within the US administration (such as those made by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in November 2016) describing Egypt as a reliable partner cooperating on national security issues. This reflects a tug-of-war between Washington’s desire to curb Chinese influence and its strategic need for cooperation with Cairo.
–            Second: Chinese Strategic and Military Analysis of the Dimensions and Consequences of Halting or Reducing US Military Aid to Egypt
1) Beijing’s View of the Impact of Reducing US Military Aid to Egypt on the Egyptian Military Arsenal: Chinese military circles believe that the Egyptian Armed Forces’ reliance on massive US systems, such as F-16 fighter jets, Abrams tanks, and Apache helicopters, requires continuous funding and logistical support from this aid.
2) Analysis by Chinese Military Think Tanks of the Financial Burden on Egypt in the Event of Reducing US Military Aid: Chinese military experts warn that any suspension or actual cessation of US military aid to Cairo will impose additional financial burdens on the Egyptian general budget to secure spare parts and maintenance for this arsenal.
In this context, the Chinese vision for the future of this American aid, its repercussions for China, and even the potential positive effects for China as a result rest on several fundamental pillars:
– First: China’s Capitalization on the Fluctuations in American Policy and Arms Controls
1) The Trust Gap as a Strategic Opportunity: Beijing recognizes that the political volatility in Washington and the frequent threats to review or suspend parts of the aid based on political conditions create a state of uncertainty for Cairo.
2) Circumventing Qualitative Restrictions: China believes that the American restrictions imposed on supplying Egypt with the latest military technologies—ostensibly to maintain Israel’s qualitative military edge—are pushing the Egyptian army to seek alternatives. Beijing capitalizes on this by providing advanced systems, such as long-range air defense systems, and by localizing defense industries without preconditions.
–             Second: Upholding the principle of diversification, not complete replacement
1) Military Realism: Chinese strategic circles recognize that the Egyptian army’s arsenal has relied for decades on extensive American systems that are difficult to replace in the short or medium term. Therefore, Beijing is not betting on cutting off American aid as much as it is betting on the erosion of Washington’s monopoly on Egyptian arms.
2) Strengthening Strategic Independence: China, as demonstrated by President Xi Jinping’s statements during his visit to Cairo, encourages countries in the region to build their security independence and reduce their sole reliance on Western powers. This aligns with Egypt’s policy of diversifying arms sources through joint exercises, such as the Civilian Eagles air exercises.
– Third: China’s Benefit from the Security Stability Provided by US Military Aid to Egypt
1) Protecting Chinese Economic Interests: From a purely economic perspective, China is not harmed by continued US military support for Egypt as long as it contributes to maintaining internal and regional stability. This stability is essential for securing Beijing’s massive investments in the Suez Canal Economic Zone and protecting trade routes associated with China’s Belt and Road Initiative.
2) Monitoring Regional Security Coordination: Beijing closely follows Egyptian-American intelligence and military coordination on issues related to de-escalating regional conflicts—such as maritime security in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz and the ceasefire in Gaza—and believes that continued US military funding keeps Cairo a pivotal player in maintaining regional balances that serve China’s commercial interests.
–             Fourth: Utilizing the Chinese rapprochement as an Egyptian bargaining chip
1) Understanding the balance of power: Beijing understands that Cairo’s military openness gives Egypt an effective bargaining chip in its negotiations with the US administration. International analyses, such as those published in the American magazine Foreign Affairs, confirm that Washington’s fears of Chinese expansion sometimes lead it to reconsider freezing aid or to expedite military deals to ensure Cairo remains within its sphere of influence.
2) Technological and training gains: China sees itself as a winner in either scenario. Even if US aid continues as the primary source of support, joint training exercises and the exchange of expertise in military academies allow Beijing to understand the combat doctrine of modern Western systems, such as the Rafale fighter jet and command and control systems, and to expand its soft power influence within the Egyptian military establishment.
In this context, although the Chinese Ministry of National Defense and the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) do not issue official statements regarding US military aid to Egypt, adhering to Beijing’s policy of non-interference and avoiding public comment on other countries’ bilateral relations, we can infer the strategic vision of the Chinese military establishment from its field operations, joint maneuvers, and reports from Chinese military and strategic research centers, as follows:

articles.title_orig: China’s Xi meets Australia’s Albanese after the APEC summit
articles.title_zh: China’s Xi meets Australia’s Albanese after the APEC summit
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese faced sharp criticism by opposition and Greens politicians after he joined a group photograph with Russian president Vladimir Putin at a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders in China despite calls to sit it out over the war in Ukraine .
Mr Albanese posed for the family photo at a gala dinner for leaders at the Apec summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on Wednesday. He stood in the back row, metres from Mr Putin, who took the centre stage alongside Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US president Donald Trump . This was Mr Putin’s first attendance at Apec in nearly a decade.
Mr Albanese said he did not want to disrespect Mr Xi as the host. He told journalists on the sidelines of the summit: "I will bear in mind the wishes of our host, but we'll also make our position very clear when it comes to Ukraine."
David Shoebridge, the Greens leader who has opposed sending military aid and weapons to Ukraine, said Mr Albanese should have taken a tougher stance.
“We are seeing the prime minister travel the world, getting mugshots with these powerful hard-right figures. One day it's Modi from India, the next day is Trump from the United States, and now it's Putin from Russia,” he told reporters.
"It's about time that he started expressing Australians' values which seem to be a very long way away from who he chooses to do his photo ops with."
The Australian Federation of Ukrainian Organisations had urged Mr Albanese not to appear in the photo, saying it would ignore Russia's gross violations of international norms. Vasyl Myroshnychenko, Ukraine's ambassador to Australia, told SBS News he hoped Mr Albanese would "continue to be guided by Australia's very prominent pro-Ukraine stance". He said: "Substance matters more to Ukraine than style."
Deputy prime minister Richard Marles defended the leader. Asked on Today whether it made him uncomfortable to see Mr Albanese "all smiles" near a man accused of war crimes, Mr Marles said Apec was a very important gathering for Australia because the vast bulk of its trade happened within the region.
"When the host puts together the family photo, you respect what the host does, but let's be really clear: Australia's position in relation to the war in Ukraine is utterly steadfast. We utterly oppose Russia's illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine, and we have stood by Ukraine. And a family photo doesn't change any of that."
Ahead of his address to the summit on Wednesday, Mr Albanese called for "more dialogue, less military conflict" in Ukraine and the Middle East .
"We do say that any solution and peace which we want to see in Ukraine needs to be on Ukraine's terms."
Mr Putin used the summit to condemn European sanctions on Moscow, which were put in place after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. He said at the summit: "Artificial barriers at one level of the value chain lead to costs across all other links." He claimed Europe was experiencing a "humiliating decline".
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky , who is absent from the summit, said in a post on social media that any issues concerning his country should be decided with his participation. He said: "This is the only approach there can ever be."
Asked whether he would follow former prime minister Tony Abbott , who said in 2014 that he would "shirtfront" Mr Putin, a term for a physical confrontation, at the G20 summit in Brisbane over the shooting down of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17, Mr Albanese said he would not take lessons in diplomacy from his predecessor. Thirty-eight Australians were killed when the plane was shot down over eastern Ukraine.
The photo preceded talks on Thursday between Mr Trump, Mr Xi and Mr Putin, the first meeting of its kind between the three leaders. The Ukraine conflict and the US-Israeli war on Iran are believed to be up for discussion.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO live: Anthropic stock begins trading in record $81B raise with $1.5T valuation
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO live: Anthropic stock begins trading in record $81B raise with $1.5T valuation
articles.content_orig:
Retail investors with access to Anthropic's initial public offering who sell the stock quickly after buying could get penalized by their brokerage firm.
Anthropic said in an IPO prospectus that it expected to make shares available to retail investors through various brokerages, including Charles Schwab , Fidelity, Robinhood , SoFi , E-Trade and some of their respective affiliates.
Follow CNBC' s live coverage of Anthropic's IPO and Nasdaq debut
These broker-dealers have "anti-flipping" policies meant to discourage investors who purchase IPO shares — including those of Anthropic — from dumping them quickly. Charles Schwab is the only one that doesn't have such a policy in place.
"One purpose is to discourage 'flippers' who are just buying with the hope of making a quick profit," Jay Ritter, director of The IPO Initiative at the University of Florida, said in an email. "Their selling could put downward pressure on the price once trading starts."
Investors who run afoul of anti-flipping rules may be prohibited from accessing future IPOs, perhaps for several months or even more than a year for repeat offenders. In the worst case, the brokerage may bar them from all future IPOs.
These policies apply only to retail investors who place an order with their brokerage firm to buy the Anthropic IPO at its offering price — something many investors don't have access to.
For example, Fidelity customers are eligible to participate in the Anthropic IPO if they have at least $25,000 in certain assets, the firm said . Even then, customers are "evaluated and ranked" based on factors such as account assets to determine who can access limited shares that may be available, it said .
Importantly, anti-flipping policies don't apply to retail investors who access shares later, once Anthropic stock starts trading on a public exchange, Ritter said.
Of the retail brokerage firms listed in Anthropic's prospectus, Charles Schwab appears to be the only one without an explicit anti-flipping policy.
"At this time, Schwab does not apply a flipping restriction to any IPOs unless required by an issuer," Margaret Farrell, a company spokesperson, wrote in an email. "This is subject to change at Schwab's discretion."
She confirmed that an anti-flipping policy doesn't apply to the Anthropic IPO.
Other firms aren't as lenient, however.
Here's how they could penalize IPO flippers.
E-Trade said it "prefers investors hold shares for at least 30 calendar days."
However, its policy doesn't lay out an explicit penalty for failing to do so.
Selling or transferring out of an IPO within 30 days "may affect eligibility to participate in other new issues in the future," according to its policy. "E*TRADE reserves the right to exclude customers from future participation."
Investors who are allocated Anthropic shares and sell within the first 15 calendar days from the start of trading in the secondary market won't be able to participate in future stock IPOs through Fidelity for a defined period of time, it said :
"The first day clients can sell without being labeled a 'flipper' is the 16th calendar day after the IPO trades," Fidelity said.
Robinhood's policy stipulates that selling IPO shares within 30 days of the IPO is considered flipping.
Such investors "may be prevented from participating in IPO access for 60 days," it said.
SoFi said that selling an IPO position within the first 30 calendar days after trading starts "may affect your ability to participate in future IPOs on SoFi."

articles.title_orig: Uncontacted Indigenous people emerge from Amazon forest to ask for food
articles.title_zh: Uncontacted Indigenous people emerge from Amazon forest to ask for food
articles.content_orig:
Along the eastern lip of the Amazon, where much of the forest has been razed for cattle ranching, there remains an island of green: the Araribóia Indigenous Territory.
Roughly twice the size of Rhode Island, the expanse in Brazil’s Maranhão state is home to three Indigenous groups and more than 10,000 people. Some of them live in complete isolation, without any contact with the outside world.

articles.title_orig: Russia Hits Three Kyiv Bridges in Overnight Ballistic Attack
articles.title_zh: Russia Hits Three Kyiv Bridges in Overnight Ballistic Attack
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russian ballistic missile strikes damaged Kyiv’s Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and South bridges early Friday, Nov. 20, prompting traffic restrictions as fires broke out across the capital.
Russian ballistic missile strikes damaged three bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv early Friday, Nov. 20, disrupting traffic between the capital’s left and right banks as fires erupted in several districts.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported damage to the Podilskyi and Darnytskyi bridges, while the South Bridge was struck again.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Traffic from the right bank to the left bank was suspended on the Podilskyi Bridge. Authorities were assessing the damage to the Darnytskyi Bridge.
The South Bridge remained partially operational, allowing vehicles traveling only from the left bank to the right bank, with weight limits of 10 tons for ordinary vehicles and 18 tons for public transport.
Klitschko urged residents to avoid unnecessary car travel and called on businesses to introduce remote work where possible.
A series of explosions rocked Kyiv overnight as Ukrainian air defenses responded to the incoming missile threat.
City authorities reported fires and damage in at least three districts: Obolonskyi, Podilskyi and Holosiivskyi.
In Obolonskyi, falling missile debris sparked a fire in a three-story building, while another building caught fire in a nonresidential area of Podilskyi.
In Holosiivskyi, a strike hit the grounds of an infrastructure facility, with preliminary reports indicating that an office building on the premises had caught fire.
The latest strikes followed Russian drone attacks on Kyiv on Thursday, Nov. 19, which killed one person and injured several others.
Thursday’s attacks also damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies and the landmark St. Volodymyr’s Cathedral, as US President Donald Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China.

articles.title_orig: Tech stocks fall as Anthropic IPO fails to stem broader AI sell-off
articles.title_zh: Tech stocks fall as Anthropic IPO fails to stem broader AI sell-off
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Japan's SoftBank Group plunged 16.16% on Friday, leading a broader sell-off in Asian technology stocks following the highly anticipated market debut of artificial intelligence startup Anthropic .
SoftBank is one of the biggest backers of OpenAI, Anthropic's rival, having invested a total of $64.6 billion in the ChatGPT maker.
The sharp decline underscores growing investor concerns over SoftBank's aggressive bets on artificial intelligence, particularly its exposure to OpenAI, as markets question whether massive investments in AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.
SoftBank's heavy exposure to OpenAI has made its shares particularly sensitive to shifts in sentiment toward the AI sector. The stock lost 30% in October and is down 31% so far this month.
If Friday's losses hold, it would be SoftBank's worst day in more than two years.
Japanese semiconductor stocks also tumbled, with Tokyo Electron falling 7.19%, Lasertec declining 6.75% and Renesas Electronics dropping 6.71%.
The sell-off extended to South Korea, where Nvidia suppliers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dropped 6% and 4.7%, respectively, pressuring the benchmark Kospi, which fell 4.6%.
Elsewhere in the region, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co , or TSMC, fell 4.76% in Taiwan.
Chinese tech giant Tencent declined 1.89%, while memory chipmaker CXMT fell 4.35% to a fresh record low, while Baidu dropped 4.42%. AI chipmaker Enflame , dubbed as one of China's " four little dragons " fell 3.93%.
The declines in Asia come after the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% overnight following Anthropic's highly anticipated Wall Street debut.

articles.title_orig: Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper hit in Houthi strike on Saudi wealth fund HQ
articles.title_zh: Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper hit in Houthi strike on Saudi wealth fund HQ
articles.content_orig:
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund , was struck on Thursday in a Houthi attack in the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Iran-backed Yemeni group.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense said a Houthi attack on a tower in Riyadh’s financial center caused material damage to several floors of the building and nearby buildings, but no injuries were reported , state news agency SPA said. The statement did not identify the tower, but an accompanying photograph published by SPA showed the PIF Tower.
The Houthis said they had targeted Riyadh’s financial center twice on Thursday, first at dawn and again in the evening.
They also said they had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Khamis Mushait airbase in southern Saudi Arabia and SADAF Petrochemical Company in Jubail in the kingdom’s Eastern Province. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of these attacks.
The kingdom’s foreign ministry said it reserved the right to take “all necessary measures” to defend its sovereignty and protect its citizens and national assets following the Houthi attack.
The strike blew out windows across seven to eight floors of the PIF Tower, bending parts of its metal facade . It was the second time in less than two weeks that a Houthi attack damaged a landmark in Riyadh’s financial district, with state oil company Aramco’s building hit in a November 8 attack.
The King Abdullah Financial District was closed to visitors following the attack.
Three sources familiar with the matter said the building had been struck by an incoming Houthi missile . The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had “dealt with a missile threat” launched towards Riyadh and that debris had fallen.
PIF, which stands for the Public Investment Fund, acknowledged receiving a Reuters request for comment. The Houthis issued no immediate statement on the strike.
The Houthis have been firing at Saudi airports and oil infrastructure since Yemen’s frozen civil war reignited in July amid the US-Iran war. On the ground in Yemen, the group has seized swathes of territory from the Saudi-backed government, forcing it to stage a major retreat at the weekend.
Residents of the Saudi capital were awoken by a loud boom in the early hours of Thursday.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense issued several warnings of potential danger in Riyadh throughout Thursday, including after the attack, before announcing that the threat had passed.
The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported that Saudi aircraft had carried out airstrikes on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital Sanaa early on Thursday, without providing further details.
Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the strikes.
The conflict has dealt a blow to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plans to develop and diversify the economy of Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter and a US ally.
The prince met US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh on Wednesday, Cooper’s third publicly reported visit to Saudi Arabia since the Yemen conflict resumed.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that Saudi officials now foresee the campaign stretching on for up to six months , according to two Western officials briefed by the Saudis on the kingdom’s plans. A third ​source familiar with the Saudi plans confirmed the accounts.
The sources said the Saudis, who replaced the commander of their coalition fighting in Yemen this week, want to see their allies make gains on the ground before they enter any negotiations with the Houthis.
Meanwhile, the situation in Yemen has appeared to favour the Houthis, who have seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast including the strategically vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its mouth, and have surrounded the city of Taiz in highlands overlooking the government’s temporary capital Aden.
In the wider war, which began in February when the United States and Israel attacked Iran , there has been no sign of a breakthrough in negotiations mediated by Qatar.
Meanwhile, there has been an uptick in hostilities in the Gulf in recent days, with Iran firing at US allies Bahrain and Kuwait and US airstrikes hitting Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
Saudi Arabia first entered the Yemen conflict in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to restore Yemen’s government to power ​after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country. They fought to a bloody stalemate and in 2022 reached a ceasefire that lasted until summer this year.

articles.title_orig: Cyberattack may have exposed Chase Bank and Mastercard customer data
articles.title_zh: Cyberattack may have exposed Chase Bank and Mastercard customer data
articles.content_orig:
Payment services were unaffected, the companies said.
JPMorganChase said Thursday morning that "third parties who provide services" to the banking giant "were the target of a cyberattack."
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," the statement continued.
"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase, the largest U.S. bank, did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party companies that were targeted.
"Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring," the company said in its statement.
JPMorganChase said on Monday that it experienced technical issues that triggered online delays across several major U.S. banks and blamed the outage on a "software bug." The company said Thursday that it found "no connection to service disruptions some customers experienced earlier this week" regarding the third-party provider data breach.
Mastercard also reported on Thursday that one of its third-party providers was hacked, while Visa said earlier this week that it was aware that one of its third-party providers experienced a data breach.
"They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific," Visa said in its statement. "Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected."
"We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of [a] limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," Mastercard said in its statement Thursday.
"There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," Mastercard further said. "At this time, the exposure has been contained, and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed."
There have been several recent tech outages across the nation that affected air travel, email and hotel reservations, and even slowed classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration officials continued this week to insist that there is no evidence that those outages were the result of cyberattacks.

articles.title_orig: UK conducting offensive cyber ops against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, top commander reveals
articles.title_zh: UK conducting offensive cyber ops against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, top commander reveals
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: China’s AI Firms Are Addicted to Nvidia Chips. Now They Are Facing Withdrawal.
articles.title_zh: China’s AI Firms Are Addicted to Nvidia Chips. Now They Are Facing Withdrawal.
articles.content_orig:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices .
"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws.
Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time.
A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies," the spokesperson said.
"The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC.
On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue.
"AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson.
The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising.
"It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four."
Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales.
The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week.
H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July.
"In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC.
The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest."
The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including ByteDance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu .
The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.
In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.
"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said.
Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS —  Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.
"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.
Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment.
Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2.
Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify.
Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third countries.
The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.
— Megan Cassella , Daren Fonda and Kif Leswing contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Kushner says he believes Russia is ‘comfortable’ with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Kushner says he believes Russia is ‘comfortable’ with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
US envoy also says he believes Moscow is ‘comfortable’ with a guarantee; Russia attacks Kyiv bridges after Putin vows response for Crimea bridge attack. What we know on day 1,731
US envoy Jared Kushner has said Donald Trump is open to extending Ukraine a security guarantee similar to Nato’s mutual defence clause , but stressed that Washington has to protect its interests too. French president Emmanuel Macron meanwhile urged Kyiv’s allies to “reopen the question” of Ukraine becoming a member of the military alliance. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, told a press conference in Germany: “From America’s perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that. We also have to make sure that it’s part of a broader security package.”
Kushner’s comments came after Ukraine’s allies gathered for a summit of the “coalition of the willing” in Berlin with Volodymyr Zelenskyy to emphasise support for Kyiv nearly five years since Russia’s 2022 invasion, and to push for a European role in future peace negotiations. Kushner added on Thursday that “we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept, where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5 ”. He noted that went with Moscow’s intention to “not have another war” when this conflict was over, while acknowledging “scepticism” over the position.
Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to do the “maximum” to deliver the air defence systems it needed, as well as looking again at Ukraine joining Nato . “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to Nato,” the French president said in Berlin. “Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he said, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
Vladimir Putin said Russia’s response to the bombing of the Kerch bridge to Crimea would be “painful” , after Ukraine attacked the strategic connection for the third time this week. The Russian president claimed he had considered agreeing to local ceasefires until the Kerch road bridge was destroyed, report Dan Sabbagh and Jakub Krupa .
On Friday, after Putin’s threat, a Russian ballistic missile attack hit three ⁠bridges on Kyiv’s Dnipro River and killed three people , the city’s mayor said, in the ⁠biggest strikes on routes ⁠connecting ​the left and right banks of Ukraine’s capital since the war began. The missiles hit the ⁠ Podilsko-Voskresenskyi bridge crossing as well as the Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges , Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram, resulting in closure or ⁠traffic restrictions. About ‌15 people were injured, he added. The strikes also caused fires ‌and damaged critical infrastructure and buildings. In the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people, mayor Igor Terekhov said.
The summit of the coalition of the willing on Thursday was co-hosted by the leaders of Germany, Britain and France shortly after unprecedented three-way talks in China between Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. China, Russia and the US said after their talks they had agreed to a peace statement, but the declaration made no mention of the war in Ukraine. The European coalition’s meeting in Berlin expressed indignation at the trilateral’s cosy optics, reports Rebecca Bailey . “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said he expected new Ukraine peace talks would “take place soon” , with Europe now set to have a seat at the table alongside the US, Russia and Ukraine. Merz, speaking in Berlin, did not give a date and added that “we are looking for locations on neutral ground”, naming the United Arab Emirates as a possible location. British prime minister Andy Burnham said: “I hope that message is heard very clearly in Moscow. For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine and we will not falter.”
A wave of daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged the historic Saint Volodymyr Cathedral as well as the embassies of Austria and the Netherlands. “Russia has been terrorising Kyiv with drones all day ... At least four people are known to be injured so far, and one person was killed,” prime minister Sergiy Koretsky said.

Fox News host Jesse Watters was aghast, amazed and a little out of pocket upon witnessing the hyper-realistic graphics featured in the newly released "Grand Theft Auto VI."
During Thursday's edition of "The Five," Watters and his co-hosts reacted to footage from the long-awaited game's extended look.

After watching the clip for the first time, Watters said he thought it was real life and that the games he grew up playing were nothing compared to "GTA VI."
"It's like I saw a clip of this the other day. And I thought it was real. Remember the guy with, like, the jacked — he's like walking through — I thought I was looking at 'The Bachelor' promo. I was like, 'Wow, this is crazy.' This is real. Can you have *** in this?" Watters said.
However, Watters seemed somewhat disappointed when his co-host, Emily Compagno, informed him that players couldn't solicit *** workers like they could in previous installments of the franchise.
"What? This game went woke?" Watters said.

"Some people are complaining about that, yes," Compagno replied.
"GTA VI" developer Rockstar Games told ShackNews that it excluded the ability to hire *** workers to focus more on the game's crime drama/romance narrative between the main protagonists, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos.
"Many aspects of previous titles are not present in GTA VI, but the elements we have we believe are all necessary and complementary to the feeling and motivations we wanted to emphasize as you play through Jason and Lucia's story," the game developer said.

articles.title_orig: World reacts to ICJ finding Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: World reacts to ICJ finding Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
The landmark judgement in The Hague on Thursday is the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide at the ICJ.
The case filed by Gambia in 2019 has been closely watched by governments, lawyers, rights groups and Rohingya communities for its implications for how states are judged under the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The court said Myanmar has an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations ‌it committed, with the terms to be determined at a later date.
Here’s how key parties and world leaders reacted to the landmark verdict:
The National Unity Government, which includes remnants of former leader Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy party, said it respects the authority of the International Court of Justice and its judgement.
It pledged to consider the court’s findings and orders, reaffirming its commitment to accountability and preventing further atrocities.
A US official told Al Jazeera that the United States was studying the ICJ’s ruling to assess its implications, while stressing the importance of preventing the court from being politicised.
“The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications,” the official said.
“We express our support for the people of Burma and share the grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups.”
The Gambia, which brought the case against Myanmar in November 2019 with the support of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, welcomed the ruling with “profound satisfaction”, calling it “a historic day for international justice”.
The government said the obligation to prevent and punish genocide is shared by all states party to the 1948 Genocide Convention and called on Myanmar to comply with the judgement “fully and without delay”.
Bangladesh has welcomed the ICJ’s ruling and urged Myanmar to implement it without delay, saying the decision could pave the way for the safe, voluntary and dignified return of Rohingya refugees.
In a statement reported by the state-run Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS) news agency, the Foreign Ministry said Myanmar was legally bound to comply with the judgement and reaffirmed that repatriation remained the only viable solution to the Rohingya crisis.
In a post shared on X, the OIC commended the ICJ’s judgement, saying it offered “redress for victims and [upholds] the principle of no impunity”.
Antonio Guterres described the ruling as a “demonstration of international justice” and a reaffirmation that impunity for “such horrific acts must not stand”.
He noted that it marked the first time the court had found a state responsible for committing genocide and called on Myanmar to comply with its decision.
The UN refugee agency (UNHCR) said the ruling was an important step towards addressing the causes of Rohingya displacement and finding lasting solutions, including access to citizenship and the creation of conditions for their safe, voluntary and dignified return.
The agency said more than 1.3 million Rohingya refugees remained displaced across the region, most of them in Bangladesh, while more than 100,000 people remained internally displaced in Myanmar’s Rakhine State.
Volker Turk said the judgement “clearly concludes” that Myanmar is responsible for “one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind.”
In a post shared on X, he added that the Rohingya people’s “suffering is a stain” on humanity.
Ed Miliband said the United Kingdom ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attache and summoned the country’s charge d’affaires. He also called for an urgent UN Security Council session to discuss the ruling.
He said further measures would be announced in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held accountable.
Yanghee Lee called it a “deeply emotional day for all Rohingya people”, adding that “justice has been decided, but not yet delivered”.
Activist Nay San Lwin said justice for the Rohingya means the restoration of their citizenship, recognition of their identity and their safe and dignified return home.
He added that their struggle would continue until those demands are met.
A coalition of 219 Rohingya and other Myanmar civil society organisations welcomed the judgement and called on the international community to ensure its full implementation.
In a joint statement published by Justice For Myanmar, the groups demanded reparations, the restoration of Rohingya citizenship and the safe return of refugees. They also called for criminal accountability for Myanmar’s military leadership, including Min Aung Hlaing.
Activist Wai Wai Nu, executive director of Women’s Peace Network, said the ruling had shattered the military’s decades-long efforts to erase Rohingya identity, deny their existence and dismiss their suffering.
“By finding that Myanmar committed genocide, ordering a guarantee of non-repetition, and ordering restitution and compensation, the world’s highest court has permanently shattered that state-sponsored lie,” she said.
The human rights group said the ruling was a “historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”.
Maria Elena Vignoli welcomed the court’s decision, calling it a “long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military”.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Has Floated NATO Membership for Ukraine in Recent Meetings
articles.title_zh: U.S. Has Floated NATO Membership for Ukraine in Recent Meetings
articles.content_orig:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments. A US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".
Zelensky's remarks came after US envoys met him and Russian President Vladimir Putin as part of US efforts to end the war between their two countries.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and currently controls most of the industrial Donbas region. Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these suggestions, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees it as unrealistic.
The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.
It is possible the US envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky recently said that the two American mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.
Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.
So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.
He said the idea was now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security in his latest remarks.
It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.
The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.
Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.
He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".
In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".
He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.
The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which US President Donald Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.
Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service , which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.
Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
Myanmar committed genocide against the country’s long-persecuted Rohingya minority, the United Nations’ top court found Thursday, an unprecedented ruling that survivors of the atrocities have waited almost a decade to hear.
The historic judgement marks the first time the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also known as the World Court, has held a state accountable for genocide in its 80-year history — and the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar.
The court’s decision — by nine votes to six — also comes at a time when the broader idea of international justice has come under fire from the Trump administration.
For the Rohingya, the ICJ’s judgment is a “turning point.”
“It is the difference between being told our history was a tragedy, and being told our history was a crime that must be answered for,” said Murshid Alam, who was just 12 years old when he was driven from his home in Myanmar’s Rakhine state.
The ICJ’s rulings are final and binding, but the court — which hears disputes between states — doesn’t have the power to enforce its decisions. Its orders, however, are sent to the UN Security Council, which could decide to implement the court’s ruling through a resolution.
Between 2016 and 2017, the military in Buddhist-majority Myanmar targeted villages and towns home to Rohingya communities, looting, burning and slaughtering their inhabitants, and expelling hundreds of thousands from the country.
CNN reporting at the time documented harrowing stories from Rohingya who saw their family members raped or killed by soldiers, and in some case their Buddhist neighbors joining in the massacres . Photos showed streams of terrified people fleeing burning villages on foot or piling into overcrowded boats as they sought to reach neighboring Bangladesh and safety.
This case against Myanmar was brought in 2019 by The Gambia, a country thousands of miles from where the killings took place, in a world-first. The United States and Canada previously declared the atrocities as genocide.
Years after more than 700,000 Rohingya fled a brutal military crackdown in Myanmar, the world’s highest court has ruled the country responsible for genocide. The verdict marks a historic moment for survivors. But CNN’s Hanako Montgomery reports many remain stranded in Bangladesh with little hope of returning home.
After seven years of weighing evidence and hearing witness testimony, the ICJ found that the scale and nature of Myanmar’s atrocities were “characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group,” presiding judge Iwasawa Yuji said during a nearly three-hour reading.
“The court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy” the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.
In its judgment, the court established the military “engaged in indiscriminate killings” and gave particular weight to the “widespread acts of sexual violence, and extreme acts of violence against children” as well as security forces’ attacks on “Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh.”
Myanmar had denied its “clearance operations” were intended to destroy the Rohingya population, and said the military was conducting legitimate counterterrorism operations against a Rohingya insurgent group. The court rejected that defense, saying the Myanmar military did not distinguish between militants and civilians.
CNN has reached out to Myanmar’s military-backed government for comment on the ruling.
Murshid Alam was a child when he was forced out of his home in Myanmar’s Rakhine state by a hail of gunfire. In the chaos of the escape, he was shot in his ear — a “terrifying experience,” he told CNN. The wound has healed, but the “secondary trauma of losing my home and seeing my community destroyed” has not.
Alam was one of more than 740,000 Rohingya people who fled to Bangladesh to escape the massacres. The sprawling refugee camps that he came of age in have since become the world’s largest, hosting more than 1.2 million people.
“Our generation has grown up in displacement. We have known nothing but statelessness,” said Alam, 22, who now works to educate and advocate for young people in the Cox’s Bazar camps as founder of the Rohingya Youth Union.
The genocide ruling, he said, “tells us that the world sees our suffering and refuses to let it be erased.”
UN human rights chief Volker Türk told CNN the judgment was “historic” and particularly striking for the way it examined “the decades of discrimination and marginalization of the Rohingya.”
Following The Gambia’s successful application to bring the case, the ICJ allowed South Africa to bring a case against Israel over its war with Hamas in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. Israel denies the genocide charge.
That has led to concerns among some the court could come into collision with the Trump administration – already on a campaign to “ dismantle ” another institution, the International Criminal Court. Last month, its UN ambassador Mike Waltz accused the ICJ of trying to lower the threshold for a genocide verdict in the Myanmar case that he claimed could potentially be “weaponized” against American soldiers.
A US State Department spokesperson told CNN in a statement Thursday they “are studying the decision to fully assess its implications.”
“The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ,” the spokesperson added.
The ICJ ordered Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingya, including to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return to their place of residence and reunification of families,” and return all property lost or damaged. It also ordered Myanmar to ensure their future protection from discrimination and persecution.
It is unlikely Myanmar will adhere. The head of the Myanmar military during the massacres, Min Aung Hlaing is now the country’s leader after he overthrew the elected government – and has dismissed the Rohingya identity as “imaginary.” His military-backed government has shown little interest in allowing Rohingya to return.
What they would return to is another question. In the Rohingya homeland of Rakhine state, the military-backed government is not in control. An ethnic armed group called the Arakan Army controls the vast majority of the state, including areas that border Bangladesh, and has been accused of widespread abuses against civilians in its areas.
The world’s deadliest sea route keeps getting busier
Meanwhile, the military has ramped up airstrikes across the state as part of its grinding civil war, dropping bombs on civilian markets and hospitals, in response to territorial losses.
Rohingya now living in the camps cannot work and face dire conditions, including trafficking, exploitation, meagre food rations, and a lack of basic education.
Alam, in the Bangladesh refugee camp, hoped the ruling could pave the way for a return to the home he fled as a young boy.
“The Rohingya do not want to live in refugee camps forever. We want to return to our homeland in Rakhine state with our rights, our citizenship, and our dignity fully restored,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Trump tells skeptical Europeans: "Putin wants to end the war"
articles.title_zh: Trump tells skeptical Europeans: "Putin wants to end the war"
articles.content_orig:
BERLIN — U.S. President Donald Trump told Ukraine’s European allies on Thursday they could save money as well as lives by ending the war with Russia, according to five European officials who were briefed on the discussion.
In a call from Air Force One on his way home from meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump lamented what he characterized as the waste of billions to provide Ukraine with weapons and cash for a conflict that is killing so many people, according to three of the European officials, who were granted anonymity to describe a private meeting.
Hours after concluding his encounters with the Russian leader and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, Trump had one message for the leaders gathered in Berlin: Putin is serious about negotiating a peace deal with Ukraine.
Momentum for a peace deal has grown in recent weeks after a flurry of diplomatic activity and intensive talks in Europe, Russia and the Middle East. Trump’s meeting in China with Xi and Putin alarmed some of Ukraine’s allies and raised fears that the U.S. president could be won over to the Russian argument that Ukraine and its European supporters have prolonged the war, which began with Russia’s 2022 invasion.
Some of the officials familiar with the call described Trump’s tone as strongly critical of Europe’s ongoing support for Kyiv, while others said he was just communicating in his usual forthright style. One person briefed on the call said the president had merely emphasized how much all countries could save if the war ended and Europe no longer had to pay for aid to Ukraine.
A U.S. official briefed on the call said any suggestion that Trump had told leaders to stop funding Ukraine was “not accurate.” The president was making his long-held view clear that he “wants to bring this conflict to a close,” the official said.
A White House official rejected characterizations of the call as critical of Europeans, saying: “President Trump called into the Coalition of the Willing meeting today and was super upbeat about the prospects for peace and praised the leaders in the room. The President emphasized that the war is extremely costly in terms of human life and financing, and everyone should all be striving for peace because it will save lives and money that can be invested in our countries’ own defenses and prosperity.”
Trump’s argument was that if the war ends, European governments could be spending their money on rebuilding Ukraine or on their own people, the U.S. official said. The president sounded “optimistic” about the prospects for peace and praised the European leaders on the call for their efforts, the official added.
When asked at a press conference following the coalition meeting in Berlin whether Trump held too rosy a view of Putin’s desire to end the war, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had talked about the “horrific” loss of life in the nearly five-year war.
Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, who attended along with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, said the U.S. president had “adamantly supported” a peaceful end to this war and this had been his message to Putin and Xi.
“He sent Jared and I here specifically to be a part of the Coalition of the Willing, and he’s given us instructions on doing everything possible to end this war and be supportive of that effort,” Witkoff told reporters in Berlin. “And what I heard from him on the call today, was that he mentioned these very same principles to the other two leaders he was meeting with.”
Kushner emphasized that Trump wanted to make a deal with Europe fully involved in the process and had asked the two U.S. envoys to travel to Berlin to “reassure people” about that. The next talks will involve Europe joining Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. at the negotiating table, Kushner said.
He added that Putin is now ready to accept the notion of security guarantees for Ukraine similar to NATO’s Article 5 — a mutual defense pledge by allies to help defend each other if one of them is attacked.
Speaking to reporters later, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was “not sure” all sides had the same understanding of Article 5 as he did. “Because what does it mean, Article 5? That there are some forces of partners on your land. So, my question is: What about American soldiers?” He said Ukraine “would be happy” if the U.S. would put bases in Ukraine “like in the Middle East.”
Germany Chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the press conference, however, that Europe is providing funding for Ukrainian defense “to enable peace negotiations in the first place and to conduct them from a position of strength.”
Merz added: “We are not providing this strong support to prolong the war. We want to end this war.”
Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Trump’s faith in Putin’s goodwill was “unshakeable” but added that he hoped this time it proved to be well-founded.
“We had a call with President Trump, who was just leaving China,” Tusk said in Berlin after the coalition meeting. “He shared his impressions of his meetings with Presidents Xi and Putin and made some remarks that sounded fairly optimistic, although I have to say they were received in the room with very cautious optimism when it comes to Putin’s and Moscow’s intentions regarding peace talks.”
“But I have to say, I’ve heard this very often from President Trump. I mean, his belief in Putin’s goodwill seems unshakable, even though so far there are no facts to support it. But it would be nice, it would be good, if it really turned out, sooner or later, that Russia was genuinely ready to engage in peace talks.”
This article has been updated with additional details. Alex Gangitano contributed to this report from Washington, James Angelos contributed from Berlin and Bartosz Brzeziński contributed from Brussels.

articles.title_orig: Men guilty of abusing Joanne Young, who was drugged and advertised for sex by husband
articles.title_zh: Men guilty of abusing Joanne Young, who was drugged and advertised for sex by husband
articles.content_orig:
A woman who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband has said she will "never feel completely safe" after four men were found guilty of sexually abusing her, in the first trial of its kind in England.
Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said: "The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way."
Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire. He invited men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to the couple's home without her knowledge.
On Thursday, Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.
Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it".
On the steps outside the court, she said: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to."
Joanne Young said the crimes committed against her had resulted in a "devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children".
She said: "I live with a pain that is hard to put into words and this is something that will affect our lives forever. It is terrifying that this could happen to anyone.
"What I have been through means I now never feel completely safe and while it can now be hard for me to leave the house, this horrific abuse showed me that home offered no protection either, even though at the time I believed I was safe."
She said the verdicts were significant "more broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men", sending the message "that you can be believed and understood".
She urged the government to look at the law of consent "as a priority" so that women were "properly protected in the future", adding her case had raised "serious questions".
In a social media post, Young's daughter Alex said it was "simply unacceptable" that the law had not been changed in England and Wales since 2003.
"Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"
Judge Mr Justice Saini had asked for calm as the verdicts were read out, with Joanne Young sitting in the public gallery surrounded by her family, her hands clasped over her mouth.
She gasped as the first guilty verdicts were read out against Connor Sanderson-Doyle, who dropped his head as he was convicted of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration.
The jury of eight men and four women also convicted Wilkins of one count of assault by penetration.
Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at a court hearing in February.
The judge commended Joanne Young and said she had shown "amazing bravery through these proceedings".
One police officer could also be seen sobbing as they left the court.
As all defendants were led from the courtroom after being told by the judge to expect lengthy jail terms when they were sentenced on 21 and 22 December, Joanne Young's family could be seen hugging.
Philip Young - who served as a Conservative Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 - drugged and raped his wife over 13 years and invited the men to have sex with her without her consent.
He pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife.
Speaking outside court, James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor, said: "This case marks the first time in England that a jury has convicted men of sexually assaulting a woman who had been drugged in abuse organised by her husband."
The crimes of the former councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.
Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.
Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.
Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.
The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.
Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.
They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".
Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.
A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.
"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.
"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."
